title: The Silencing of the Schools
subtitle: The fall of the Old Scholastic Coast and the Flight of the Scholars
summary: How an older Kharadi regime closed the schools of the Scholastic Coast, why its scholars fled to Verna, and why Kharadis and Vernans still argue over the manuscripts.
content:
> *"Take the pages. Leave the bindings."*
> — attributed by Vernan tradition to the librarians of the Coast

The **Silencing of the Schools** is the name [Verna](factions.html#verna) gives to what followed the conquest of the **Old Scholastic Coast** by an older Kharadi regime: the closing of its schools, the seizure and burning of its libraries, and the persecution of its scholars and heterodox faiths. It is one of the defining events in the history of two peoples. For Verna, it is the reason the University of Verna became what it is. For the [Kharad Compact](factions.html#kharad-compact), it is a crime committed by a state that was not the Compact, in the name of a faith the Compact still holds, and modern Kharadis are still arguing about what that means.

This entry belongs to both of them, and tries to be fair to both.

## The Old Scholastic Coast

Before its conquest, the **Old Scholastic Coast** was a string of cities famous for **philosophy**, **mathematics**, **medicine**, **astronomy**, **rhetoric** and **natural philosophy**. The cities were not necessarily united politically, and they quarrelled with each other as cities do. Culturally, though, they were the great centres of learning of their age. To say someone had *studied on the Coast* was close to saying they were a serious scholar.

The Coast was also a place of many voices: competing philosophical schools, old temples, heterodox religious traditions, sceptical thinkers, foreign beliefs and libraries that held almost everything.

The names of most of its cities, and the details of its history, are themselves among the things the Silencing damaged. The Archive does not yet hold a reliable list.

## The Conquest

At some point in the past, the state that ruled Kharadi lands became more expansionist, more centralised and more religiously aggressive than its people had been before or have been since. That older regime, which was not the modern Compact, conquered the Old Scholastic Coast. When exactly it happened, and what the regime called itself, are not recorded in the Archive's sources.

The conquest was not only political. The regime set out to impose **religious and intellectual conformity** on the Coast, and the Coast was everything such a regime could not tolerate.

## The Silencing

What followed is what Verna remembers as **the Silencing of the Schools**:

- schools were **closed**;
- temples were **closed or converted**;
- archives were **seized**;
- books were **destroyed**;
- teachers were **required to renounce** forbidden doctrines;
- some intellectual and religious communities were **persecuted**.

People responded as people do. Some complied. Some hid what they could. Some were killed. Many fled. How long the Silencing lasted, and how many it touched, are not known with any precision.

> **From an order of closure, as preserved in a Vernan archive**
>
> *By the authority of the Governor of the Coast, and in accordance with the true teaching:*
>
> *The school known as the House of the Northern Stair is closed. Its masters are to present themselves before the examiners by the third day. Its books are to be surrendered entire to the officers of inspection, who will determine which may be preserved.*
>
> *Those who conceal books, or teach privately what has been forbidden publicly, will answer for it.*
>
> *There is one truth, and it does not require debate.*

That last line is the one Vernan teachers make their students copy out.

## The Flight of the Scholars

A great many of those who fled went to **Verna**, a small republic nearby. They included professors, physicians, mathematicians, librarians, scribes, translators, students, instrument-makers, patrons and whole families. They carried whatever they could: manuscripts, charts, scientific instruments, partial archives and, perhaps most importantly, ways of teaching that could not be confiscated because they lived in people's heads.

> **From a Vernan collection of refugee testimonies**
>
> *My mother was a copyist in the library of the Lower School. When the inspectors came to the city, she did not try to save the books. She knew she could not carry them.*
>
> *She saved the pages.*
>
> *She cut the most important ones out of their bindings with a penknife and sewed them flat into the lining of her winter coat, and into mine, and into the grain sacks on the cart. "Take the pages," she told the others. "Leave the bindings. Bindings are for libraries. We are not a library any more."*
>
> *I wore forty pages of geometry across the border. I was nine. I did not know what was in my coat until we reached Verna and she cut it open on the kitchen table.*

Verna already existed, and it already had colleges. The refugees did not found it. What they did was make its scholarly institutions much larger and far more important, until they grew into the federation of colleges, archives and laboratories known today as the [[verna-and-the-university|University of Verna]].

## Modern Kharad and the Silencing

The modern Compact does not speak with one voice about the Silencing, and it would be wrong to say it defends it.

Many Kharadi scholars condemn it outright, as an atrocity committed by an earlier regime. Some of the sharpest condemnations are religious. The old conquerors, they argue, violated the [[covenant-of-the-one|Covenant]] itself: they used political and religious power to justify an unequal Measure, one law for the faithful conqueror and another for the conquered scholar. *Do not make two measures where the One gave one.*

Others are more defensive. They argue that modern people cannot inherit unlimited liability for the crimes of their ancestors, that the regime that did this no longer exists, and that the Compact has spent generations being something very different. Some go further, and quietly revise the story. Every one of these positions has defenders in Kharadi universities and temples, and the argument is very much alive.

> **From a lecture at a Kharadi academy, as a student recorded it**
>
> "You will hear it said that the conquerors were simply men of their time. Write that down, so that you can recognise it later as an excuse.
>
> "They had the Recitation. They had Nahira, who would not burn incense to the powerful. They knew that power does not make a thing right. They burned the libraries anyway, and they did it in the name of the One.
>
> "That is not a stain on the Covenant. It is a betrayal of it. And we are the ones who still keep the Covenant, so we are the ones who must say so."

## The Question of Restitution

Some Kharadi institutions still hold manuscripts, temple objects, scientific instruments, artworks and archives that were taken from the Scholastic Coast. Verna argues that they should be returned.

The holders have answers. They point out that these objects have been preserved for centuries, often carefully, when they might otherwise have been lost. They argue that modern ownership is legally established, and that the provenance of many pieces is genuinely disputed. The legal status of the disputed objects is not settled, and the question surfaces in diplomacy, scholarship and, increasingly, in auction houses.

> **A conversation in a reading room, as the Vernan curator later described it**
>
> "We agree that the conquest was a crime," said the Kharadi archivist.
>
> "We do."
>
> "We agree that the pages in this case were taken from a school on the Coast."
>
> "Almost certainly from the Northern Stair."
>
> "And we agree that if they had stayed where they were, they would have burned with everything else."
>
> "We do." The curator did not take his eyes off the case. "None of that tells me why they are in your city and not in mine."
>
> The archivist was quiet for a moment. "No," she said. "It doesn't."

## Verna and Kharad Today

The two peoples are not enemies. Trade continues. Scholarly exchange exists: Kharadi students study in Verna, and Vernan scholars visit Kharadi libraries. But Verna remains wary of Kharadi debt, financial dependency, patronage and influence, and that wariness is historical as much as political. A small republic that was rebuilt by people fleeing a Kharadi conquest does not easily forget it.

The best description of the relationship is the one diplomats use: **distant, complicated and functional**.

## Why It Matters in Endros

The Silencing shapes the Gate era in quieter ways than war. It is part of why the University of Verna insists on independence from states and patrons, why it copies its rarest documents and stores them in more than one place, and why it is so careful about who controls what it learns. It is part of why Vernan Expeditioners ask where an artifact came from before they ask what it does. And it is why a manuscript, an instrument or a temple object of uncertain provenance can still turn up in Endros and start an argument nobody expected.
